title: Interop checksuite: ledger consistency for multipart client-side rewrites and resume semantics
creator: Ava Martinez
description:
Background: We continue to see latent discrepancies in the metering ledger when client-side prompt rewrites (proxies, SDKs) and compressed multipart uploads interact with resume semantics on unstable websocket connections. Symptoms range from small negative adjustments during finalization (where a resumed chunk causes earlier credits to be rolled back) to transient overcharges when an intermediate proxy alters encoded lengths without corresponding canonicalization upstream.

Goal: Build an interop checksuite and minimal remediation flow that validates end-to-end ledger invariants across the common rewrite paths (SDK-side prompt modifiers, proxy tokenizers, multipart compression, attachment re-encodings). The checksuite should exercise resume/abort/replay flows against the production metering pipeline and produce deterministic, auditable traces for every credit/debit event.

Deliverables: 1) automated checksuite harness (simulated clients + configurable proxies) that emits ledger traces and assertion failures; 2) a small set of canonicalization rules and lightweight server-side normalizer for encoded-length reconciliation; 3) monitoring alerts for invariant violations and a playbook for live incident triage.
acceptance_criteria: Checksuite can reproduce three known failure modes deterministically in CI: negative-finalization, duplicate-credit-on-replay, and mismatch-after-proxy-rewrite
For a representative matrix (2 SDK versions x 2 proxy behaviors x 3 resume patterns) the ledger trace must reconcile to zero-drift within 10s of finalization for all runs
Server-side normalizer accepts 'canonical-length' and 'source-hash' hints from clients and fixes at most 1% of live requests without changing observed customer output
Telemetry dashboards and an alert rule detect invariant breaches and fire a P99 alert that includes the failing trace id and client hints
steps: Design checksuite harness: define simulation scenarios (initial, resume-with-overwrite, truncated-replay, proxy-encoded-rewrite)
Implement client simulator that can 1) emit partial WS frames, 2) perform local prompt rewrite, 3) send compressed multipart payloads with altered content-length fields
Create proxy shim that can be toggled to perform typical rewrite behaviors (strip metadata, re-encode attachments, change content-length header)
Instrument metering pipeline to emit per-stage ledger events with immutable trace-id and optional client-supplied source-hash
Run the checksuite in isolated staging against a snapshot of the ledger aggregator and iterate on normalizer heuristics
Ship server-side normalizer behind feature flag and run canary traffic with end-to-end assertions
Add dashboard cards, an alert rule, and include the playbook in runbooks/confluence
telemetry: request_traces.sample - include ledger events, client hints, and raw client-encoded-lengths
test_plan: Unit tests for canonicalizer and length-normalizer logic
Integration tests: checksuite runs for matrix of SDK versions + proxies, assert zero-drift within timeout
Chaos test: inject duplicate WS frames and simulate client reconnects to ensure idempotent ledger entries
Regression: add fuzzing jobs that mutate multipart boundaries and ensure no negative balances
rollout_plan: Step 1: land checksuite + instrumentation in staging and run nightly full-matrix for 72 hours
Step 2: deploy normalizer behind feature flag, enable for 2% of traffic with strict logging
Step 3: expand to 25% after 48h if invariant violations drop >= 95% in canary group
Step 4: full rollout with monitoring and rollback playbook ready
notes: We want the checksuite assertions to be conservative; when in doubt surface a warning trace rather than auto-correct unless we have a source-hash match
Avoid changing customer-observed tokens: normalizer only adjusts encoded-length and emits a provenance marker
This work complements existing stream reconciliation initiatives but focuses on cross-process semantic mismatches caused by rewrites (not sampling-related duplicates)
